title: Review: All Letters, Letter Names vs. Sounds, b/d/p/q
goal: Consolidate all 26 letters and their sounds; explicitly separate letter *name* from letter *sound*; directly address the b/d/p/q mirror-confusion as its own short, dedicated lesson.
newToday: no new letter-sounds — this is a consolidation lesson, plus one genuinely new skill: telling b/d/p/q apart reliably.
time: 25–30 minutes (slightly longer — this is a full review lesson), single sitting.

heart.note: n (✓) is regular. The **o** says its long /oʊ/ sound, same pattern as "go" (L1.12) and "do" (L1.10) — **heart part: the "o."** Point out this is now the *third* heart word with exactly this same irregular-o pattern; naming the pattern itself is worth doing explicitly.

s (✓) is regular. Same long-o pattern again — **heart part: the "o."** By now the learner may start predicting this pattern in new words before being told; if so, say so — that's exactly the self-teaching mechanism this whole course is built on (`research/01`, Share's Self-Teaching Hypothesis).

A.text: Bob has a big dog. Pat has a big pig. The dog and the pig run. Did the dog win? Did the pig win? No, they did not win. It was a big mess.

B.text: Dan has a big box. Pat has a big box. The tag said "b." Dan said, "d?" No, it was "b." It was a big mess at the dock.

questions: What raced, in Track A, and who won?
What letter did Dan misread in Track B, and for which letter?
Think: now that you know the b/d/p/q tricks from §3, which one would have helped Dan avoid his mistake?

listen.title: Why Labels Matter
listen.passage: In busy warehouses, a single misread letter on a shipping label can send a package hundreds of miles in the wrong direction. That's why professional warehouse workers are trained to read labels a specific, careful way: never glance quickly at a whole word and guess, but check the exact letters, especially any that could be confused with another — b and d, or the number 0 and the letter O. Some warehouses even print certain confusable letters in a special typeface designed to make them look as different from each other as possible. It's a small design choice built entirely around a very human, very ordinary reading mistake.

tier2.def: a particular style or design of printed letters.
tier2.full: a particular style or design of printed letters. "This typeface makes the numbers easier to tell apart." "Formal documents often use a plain, clear typeface." Your turn: have you noticed a typeface that was especially easy or hard to read?

tier2.def: trained and skilled at a particular job, doing it to a high standard.
tier2.full: trained and skilled at a particular job, doing it to a high standard. "A professional driver checks mirrors constantly." "She gave a professional, careful answer." Your turn: what makes someone act "professionally" at a task?

questions: Why does the passage say warehouse workers are trained not to "glance quickly and guess" at labels?
What did some warehouses design specifically to solve the b/d mix-up problem?
